summary: Discusses how the RPL routing protocol for low-power, lossy networks applies to smart-metering networks (AMI). It describes how RPL features fit that setting.

eli5.summary: Smart meters across a city need to pass readings along through each other. This explains how a routing method for tiny, flaky radios works for those meters.

questions: what is rpl in smart metering
what trickle settings does rpl use for smart meters
subtitle: How the RPL routing protocol should be configured for smart-meter mesh networks run by utilities.

tldr.problem: Utilities connect millions of meters over low-power, lossy wireless and power-line links. RPL is a general-purpose protocol for such networks, so deployments need guidance on which of its options to use.
tldr.mechanism: This applicability statement profiles RPL non-storing mode for AMI: it picks RPL features, requires link-layer security, sets 6LoWPAN and Trickle defaults, and recommends parameter values.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that gives AMI vendors a common RPL profile. It covers electric meters and leaves battery-powered meters and storing mode out of scope.

today: RFC 8036 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2017, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the applicability statement for RPL non-storing mode in electric-meter AMI networks.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) systems measure, configure and control energy, gas and water consumption through two-way scheduled, on-exception and on-demand communication. AMI networks contain millions of endpoints, including meters, distribution automation elements and, eventually, Home Area Network (HAN) devices. They are linked by wireless and power line communications into a Neighbor Area Network (NAN), with a backhaul network leading to the utility's back office.

This document is an applicability statement for RPL (RFC 6550) in such networks. It covers RPL non-storing mode for electric meters. Three things are out of scope: networks of battery-powered gas and water meters, networks mixing electric and battery-powered meters, and RPL storing mode.
sections.eli5: Utilities have a huge number of meters that must report back. This RFC says how one routing method should be used for the electric ones.

sections.title: RPL and AMI Networks
sections.content:
RPL provides routing for mesh networks that scale to thousands of resource-constrained devices connected by low-power, lossy links. It builds a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) rooted at an LLN Border Router (LBR), ensures loop-free routing, and supports alternate routes and many routing metrics.

Electric meter networks may hold millions of smart meters. Each is limited in processing, storage and bandwidth, giving effective link throughput of tens to a few hundred kilobits per second, part of which security overhead can consume. Meters form multi-hop meshes that reach the utility network through an aggregation point such as an LBR.

A routing domain typically spans groups of meters in the order of 1,000 to 10,000, so a mesh has several thousand wireless endpoints. Paths to the nearest LBR may take several hops or even several tens of hops. Because electric meters are mains powered, they can afford the resources needed to route packets.
sections.eli5: Thousands of meters near each other form a team. Messages hop from meter to meter until they reach a boss box that connects to the utility.

sections.title: Smart Grid Traffic and Requirements
sections.content:
Most smart-metering traffic flows between meters and a few head-end servers at the utility. Meters send data on a schedule, on demand, or after local events such as an outage. This makes traffic highly asymmetric, flowing mostly from meters toward the LBR. Head-end traffic is either unicast to one meter or multicast to a group, and can be a small read request or a large firmware download.

The RFC lists five priority classes, each needing 98%+ packet delivery:

  • C1: outage, pricing and emergency messages, under 5 s (payload under 100 bytes).
  • C2: power quality events and service connect or disconnect, under 10 s (under 150 bytes).
  • C3: faults, configuration and security events, under 30 s (under 200 bytes).
  • C4: recurrent meter reading, a 2-hour window 6 times per day (under 400 bytes).
  • C5: firmware and software updates reaching 98%+ of devices within 7 days (average update 1 MB).

RPL non-storing mode supports unicast traffic up and down the DODAG. Group communication requires downstream multicast with scope larger than link-local, injected only by the DODAG root. Section 6 maps functional requirements from RFC 5548 to RPL features: scalability, zero-touch configuration through DIO messages, and tolerance of time-varying links using metrics such as ETX and multiple DAG parents.
sections.eli5: Some messages, like a power outage alert, must arrive in seconds. Others, like a monthly update, can take days. The network has to handle all of them.

sections.title: Layer-2 Technologies
sections.content:
The RFC assumes two main link types. Wireless NANs use IEEE 802.15.4 with the 802.15.4g physical layer and the 802.15.4e MAC amendment. Narrowband power line communication (PLC) uses IEEE 1901.2, and networks can mix both to improve coverage.

  • IEEE 802.15.4g: FSK, OQPSK and OFDM modes, with speeds from 50 kbps to 600 kbps in the overview. The PHY frame payload can carry up to 2048 octets, enough for a full IPv6 packet of 1280 octets without upper-layer fragmentation. The RFC says the MAC frame payload MUST be able to carry such a packet.
  • IEEE 1901.2: low-frequency (below 500 kHz) narrowband PLC with bit rates scalable up to 500 kbps. It prepends a Segment Control Field to the 802.15.4 MAC header and uses only 16-bit and 64-bit MAC addresses. Its PHY MTU varies with the modulation, and it uses an adaptive tone map to track link quality.

Section 7.2.3 describes 802.15.4 link security: authentication, integrity, confidentiality and freshness checks against replay. AES-CCM-32 is noted as the most commonly used suite in these deployments.
sections.eli5: Meters talk either by radio or through the power wires. Both are slow and noisy, but each can still carry a normal internet packet.

sections.title: The RPL Profile
sections.content:
Section 7 chooses how AMI deployments use RPL features.

  • Instances: one RPL instance is defined, but several may run in multi-service networks, such as one carrying both metering and distribution automation traffic.
  • DAO policy: because two-way communication is required, nodes SHOULD send DAO messages to set up downward paths.
  • Metrics and objective function: the ETX metric from RFC 6551 suits lossy links. Objective Function 0 (RFC 6552) and MRHOF (RFC 6719) are both suitable.
  • Repair: deployments SHOULD use RPL local repair. A detached node advertises an infinite rank (poisoning) so its children can pick another parent. A non-zero DAGMaxRankIncrease limits count-to-infinity costs.
  • Multicast: support for non-storing mode is being developed in companion RFCs, citing RFC 7731.
  • 6LoWPAN: all IPv6 header and next-header compression schemes of RFC 6282 can be used when reducing overhead matters.
sections.eli5: RPL has many switches. This RFC says which ones to flip on for meters, such as keeping track of how many tries a path needs and finding a new neighbor when a link breaks.

sections.title: Recommended Defaults
sections.content:
Trickle (RFC 6206) paces the sending of DIO messages. Meter density ranges from a handful of neighbors to several hundred, and a low Imin in dense areas can cause short bursts of congestion. The RFC therefore recommends more conservative values than RFC 6206, expressed relative to how long a link-local multicast packet takes to send.

  • DIOIntervalMin: set so that Imin is at least 50 times that transmit time.
  • DIOIntervalDoublings: set so that Imax is at least 2 hours.
  • DIORedundancyConstant: at least 10.
  • MinHopRankIncrease: 256, giving 8 bits of resolution for ETX.
  • MaxRankIncrease: a value allowing a small number of hops away from the root; with 256, a value of 1024 allows up to 4 hops.

For manageability, all DIO messages SHOULD contain a Metric Container option, and a DODAG Configuration option SHOULD carry the Trickle parameters, so the root can tune the network after bring-up.
sections.eli5: If every meter in a crowded block shouted updates at once, the airwaves would jam. The RFC suggests slower, calmer timing so messages do not collide.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
AMI networks sit in places with no physical security and are treated as critical infrastructure. They typically use link-layer, transport-layer and application-layer security, so RPL's own security mechanisms may not be needed. The RFC still requires that deployments MUST include at least link-layer security such as that defined by IEEE 1901.2 and IEEE 802.15.4.

Meters are loaded with keys and certificates at manufacture and use them to authenticate and negotiate operational credentials. A failed or compromised device is replaced, and the new one does not inherit the old identity. The RFC points to RFC 7416 for RPL threats and says RFC 6550 security considerations apply. For privacy, it defers to external documents it cites.
sections.eli5: Meters sit outside where anyone can touch them, so every message must be locked. Each meter gets its own key before it leaves the factory.
